title: Acid Corrosion Creating Micro-Cracks in Aluminum Barriers
introduction: Acetic acid vapor generated by degrading EVA encapsulant diffuses through the module interior and contacts aluminum metallization layers embedded in backsheet constructions. The acetic acid reacts with the aluminum, forming aluminum acetate and initiating corrosion of the metal surface. This corrosion produces small crystal deposits, increased surface porosity, and the formation of small holes. Over time these holes enlarge and interconnect into pinholes and micro-cracks that penetrate the aluminum layer, destroying its function as a barrier to further acetic acid permeation through the backsheet.
reasoning: The 657-Elsevier study documents this chemical corrosion mechanism using REM-EDX and FTIR-ATR spectroscopy, confirming that acetic acid reacts with aluminum to produce crystal deposits, pores, and micro-cracks that compromise the barrier function.

key_findings.claim: Acetic acid reacts with the aluminum barrier layer to form aluminum acetate and small crystal deposits, initiating surface corrosion
key_findings.detail: When acetic acid vapor contacts the aluminum layer in a PV backsheet, corrosion occurs producing small crystal formations and small holes in the surface. [^elsevier657a] The formation of aluminum acetate in the corrosion products was verified by spectroscopic analysis, confirming a chemical reaction between acetic acid and aluminum as responsible for the observed surface degradation. [^elsevier657b]

key_findings.claim: Aluminum corrosion confirmed by REM-EDX and FTIR-ATR spectroscopy creates pinholes and micro-cracks that enhance acid transport
key_findings.detail: Corrosion of the aluminum barrier layer by acetic acid has been confirmed by REM-EDX and FTIR-ATR spectroscopy. The corrosion creates pinholes and micro-cracks in the aluminum layer. [^elsevier657c] Additionally, increased surface porosity from small hole formation was observed, indicating progressive degradation of the aluminum barrier that allows enhanced acid permeation. [^elsevier657d]
